title: Italian grammar A2: everyday stories and choices

sources.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), communicative competence descriptors
Treccani, Indicativo passato prossimo (La grammatica italiana)

units.title: Completed past
units.description: Tell a short account of completed actions with the right auxiliary and participle.

lessons.title: Build regular completed past
lessons.outcome: I can form passato prossimo with avere and regular participles across three verb families.
lessons.takeaway: Present avere + participle reports a completed event; -ato, -uto, -ito are the regular endings.

objectives.label: Build regular completed past
objectives.explanation: Present avere + participle reports a completed event; -ato, -uto, -ito are the regular endings.

teach.title: The two-part form
teach.body: Use present avere plus the participle. The auxiliary changes with the person; the participle normally stays in its base form with avere.

examples.en: We spoke with the doctor.

teach.title: Three participle endings
teach.body: Parlare → parlato; ricevere → ricevuto; finire → finito. A time word can make the finished event clear.

examples.en: Yesterday I finished the book.

teach.tip: Some common verbs have irregular participles, taught next.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday we worked until late.
questions.explanation: Lavorare uses avere here; the completed action is abbiamo lavorato.
questions.hint: Use the we form of avere.
questions.speak: Ieri noi abbiamo lavorato fino a tardi.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Marta received a message yesterday.
questions.explanation: Ricevere forms ricevuto and takes avere for receiving something.
questions.speak: Marta ha ricevuto un messaggio ieri.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: They finished the work.
questions.explanation: Hanno finito reports a completed action by they.
questions.hint: Put the auxiliary before the participle.
questions.speak: Hanno finito il lavoro.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: You received a letter this morning.
questions.explanation: Ricevere takes the regular participle ricevuto, with avere.
questions.speak: Tu hai ricevuto una lettera stamattina.

lessons.title: Use essere in the past
lessons.outcome: I can form passato prossimo with essere and make its participle agree with the subject.
lessons.takeaway: With verbs such as andare and arrivare, use essere; the participle matches the subject.

objectives.label: Use essere in the past
objectives.explanation: With verbs such as andare and arrivare, use essere; the participle matches the subject.

teach.title: The auxiliary essere
teach.body: Some common intransitive verbs use essere: sono andato, siamo arrivati. Learn the auxiliary with the verb.

examples.en: Marco arrived at nine.

teach.title: Subject agreement
teach.body: With essere, -o/-a/-i/-e show masculine/feminine and singular/plural. A female speaker says sono andata.

examples.it: Anna e Sara sono partite presto.
examples.en: Anna and Sara left early.

teach.tip: The participle agrees with the subject, not the destination.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Sara went to Rome yesterday.
questions.explanation: Andare takes essere; andata agrees with Sara.
questions.speak: Sara è andata a Roma ieri.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: With essere, the participle agrees with the subject’s gender and number.
questions.hint: Match -a, -i, and -e endings to their subjects.
questions.speak: Sara è andata a scuola.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: We women returned home.
questions.explanation: Siamo tornate agrees with an all-female we.
questions.speak: Siamo tornate a casa.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: I, Giulia, left early.
questions.explanation: Partire takes essere and a female speaker uses partita.
questions.speak: Io, Giulia, sono partita presto.

lessons.title: Recall common participles
lessons.outcome: I can use frequent irregular participles for completed events.
lessons.takeaway: High-frequency past participles include fatto, detto, visto, letto, and preso.

objectives.label: Recall common participles
objectives.explanation: High-frequency past participles include fatto, detto, visto, letto, and preso.

teach.title: Learn the whole word
teach.body: Fare → fatto, dire → detto, vedere → visto. These completed events commonly take avere.

examples.en: I saw Marco at the market.

teach.title: More everyday forms
teach.body: Leggere → letto, prendere → preso, scrivere → scritto. Keep the auxiliary before the participle.

examples.en: Giulia wrote a letter.

teach.tip: Do not attach regular -uto to an irregular participle.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday Luca made dinner.
questions.explanation: Fare has the participle fatto.
questions.speak: Ieri Luca ha fatto la cena.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: We saw the film last night.
questions.explanation: Vedere commonly uses visto with avere.
questions.speak: Noi abbiamo visto il film ieri sera.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Did you read the message?
questions.explanation: Letto is the common participle of leggere.
questions.speak: Hai letto il messaggio?

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Marta told the truth.
questions.explanation: Dire has the participle detto, with avere here.
questions.speak: Marta ha detto la verità.

lessons.title: Choose the past auxiliary
lessons.outcome: I can choose the auxiliary from a verb’s pattern, including common movement exceptions.
lessons.takeaway: All transitive verbs use avere; many intransitives use essere, but movement alone is not a rule.

objectives.label: Choose the past auxiliary
objectives.explanation: All transitive verbs use avere; many intransitives use essere, but movement alone is not a rule.

teach.title: Object-taking verbs
teach.body: A verb acting directly on an object takes avere: ho comprato il pane, abbiamo preso il treno.

examples.en: Anna bought bread.

teach.title: Learn intransitives individually
teach.body: Andare and arrivare take essere, but camminare and viaggiare use avere. Always learn the auxiliary with the verb.

examples.en: We walked for an hour.

teach.tip: Do not choose essere merely because someone moves.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday Marco took the train.
questions.explanation: Prendere has a direct object, il treno, so use avere.
questions.speak: Ieri Marco ha preso il treno.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday the female friends went to the park.
questions.explanation: Andare takes essere and the participle agrees with amiche.
questions.speak: Ieri le amiche sono andate al parco.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: We travelled by train.
questions.explanation: Viaggiare uses avere despite expressing movement.
questions.speak: Abbiamo viaggiato in treno.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Transitive comprare and intransitive camminare use avere; arrivare uses essere, here for a female speaker.
questions.hint: Match each auxiliary with a natural completed event.
questions.speak: Ho comprato un biglietto.

units.title: Past background and action in progress
units.description: Show what used to happen, what happened once, and what was in progress.

lessons.title: Describe past habits and states
lessons.outcome: I can form common imperfect forms for repeated actions and background states.
lessons.takeaway: The imperfect uses -avo/-evo/-ivo patterns; essere has ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

objectives.label: Describe past habits and states
objectives.explanation: The imperfect uses -avo/-evo/-ivo patterns; essere has ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

teach.title: Repeated past actions
teach.body: For a past routine, use forms such as parlavo, parlavi, parlava; the plural gives parlavamo, parlavate, parlavano.

examples.it: Da bambino giocavo nel parco ogni giorno.
examples.en: As a child I played in the park every day.

teach.title: Past descriptions
teach.body: Use the imperfect for past states and background: era, avevo, faceva. It does not itself mark a finished boundary.

examples.en: Yesterday at eight I was tired.

teach.tip: Essere is irregular in the imperfect: ero, not essevo.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Da piccoli noi ___ spesso a casa dei nonni.
questions.translation: When we were small, we often ate at our grandparents’ home.
questions.explanation: Spesso and da piccoli frame a past habit; noi takes mangiavamo.
questions.speak: Da piccoli noi mangiavamo spesso a casa dei nonni.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Avevo, avevamo, and avevano describe past states for different subjects.
questions.hint: Match the subject to the imperfect ending.
questions.speak: Io avevo un cane da piccolo.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: As a girl I used to read every evening.
questions.explanation: Leggevo with ogni sera expresses a repeated past habit.
questions.speak: Da bambina leggevo ogni sera.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Ieri alle otto Marta ___ a casa.
questions.translation: Yesterday at eight Marta was at home.
questions.explanation: Era is the imperfect of essere for one person.
questions.speak: Ieri alle otto Marta era a casa.

lessons.title: Contrast background and event
lessons.outcome: I can choose imperfect for an ongoing background and passato prossimo for a completed event.
lessons.takeaway: The imperfect sets the scene; passato prossimo marks the bounded event in it.

objectives.label: Contrast background and event
objectives.explanation: The imperfect sets the scene; passato prossimo marks the bounded event in it.

teach.title: Background plus arrival
teach.body: Use imperfect for an action already underway and passato prossimo for the event that occurred: leggevo quando è arrivato.

examples.en: I was reading when Marco arrived.

teach.title: Habit versus one occasion
teach.body: Ogni sabato is often a past habit; sabato scorso can point to one completed occasion. Time words help but meaning decides.

examples.it: Sabato scorso ho letto tutto il libro.
examples.en: Last Saturday I read the whole book.

teach.tip: A single sentence can combine both tenses.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Mentre io ___, il telefono ha suonato.
questions.translation: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
questions.explanation: Mentre introduces the action in progress; the ring is the completed event.
questions.hint: Use imperfect for the background cooking.
questions.speak: Mentre io cucinavo, il telefono ha suonato.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday Anna arrived at nine.
questions.explanation: A single arrival at a stated time is a completed event.
questions.speak: Ieri Anna è arrivata alle nove.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: It was raining when we went out.
questions.explanation: Pioveva is the background; siamo usciti is the bounded action.
questions.speak: Pioveva quando siamo usciti.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Da bambino io ___ al mare ogni estate.
questions.translation: As a child I used to go to the sea every summer.
questions.explanation: Ogni estate frames a repeated past habit, so andavo.
questions.hint: Use imperfect, not a single trip.
questions.speak: Da bambino io andavo al mare ogni estate.

lessons.title: Focus on an action now
lessons.outcome: I can use stare + gerund for an action in progress now and avoid it for ordinary habits.
lessons.takeaway: Sto leggendo focuses on the current unfolding action; the simple present remains normal for habits and states.

objectives.label: Focus on an action now
objectives.explanation: Sto leggendo focuses on the current unfolding action; the simple present remains normal for habits and states.

teach.title: Build the present progressive
teach.body: Conjugate stare and add -ando for -are or -endo for -ere/-ire: sto parlando, stai leggendo.

examples.en: Right now I am reading a letter.

teach.title: Know its limit
teach.body: Use the simple present for routines and stable possession: leggo ogni sera, ho due sorelle. Italian does not need the progressive whenever English uses “-ing.”

examples.it: Leggo ogni sera prima di dormire.
examples.en: I read every evening before sleep.

teach.tip: Do not say sto avendo for ordinary possession.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Right now Luca is writing an email.
questions.explanation: Luca takes sta; scrivere gives scrivendo for the action underway.
questions.hint: Use third-person stare plus a gerund.
questions.speak: Adesso Luca sta scrivendo una mail.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Every morning I eat at seven.
questions.explanation: Ogni mattina is a habitual routine, so the simple present is natural.
questions.hint: A repeated habit uses the plain present.
questions.speak: Ogni mattina io mangio alle sette.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: We are waiting for the train now.
questions.explanation: Stiamo + aspettando focuses on the current wait.
questions.speak: Stiamo aspettando il treno.

questions.prompt: Use stare + gerundio to type the missing phrase.
questions.context: In questo momento loro ___ la cena.
questions.translation: At this moment they are preparing dinner.
questions.explanation: Loro takes stanno; preparare gives preparando.
questions.hint: Use the they form of stare plus -ando.
questions.speak: In questo momento loro stanno preparando la cena.

lessons.title: Focus on an action underway then
lessons.outcome: I can use stavo/stava/stavamo + gerund for an action underway at a past moment.
lessons.takeaway: The past progressive uses imperfect stare + gerund; it often provides the background to a completed event.

objectives.label: Focus on an action underway then
objectives.explanation: The past progressive uses imperfect stare + gerund; it often provides the background to a completed event.

teach.title: The past viewpoint
teach.body: Stavo parlando means I was speaking at a particular past moment; stava, stavamo, and other imperfect forms change with the subject.

examples.en: At eight I was studying.

teach.title: Background and interruption
teach.body: Combine it with a completed event: stavamo cenando quando è arrivata Giulia. For a repeated habit, use a plain imperfect.

examples.it: Stavamo cenando quando è arrivata Giulia.
examples.en: We were having dinner when Giulia arrived.

teach.tip: Avoid a perfect form of stare + gerund for this meaning.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: At nine Marta was reading a book.
questions.explanation: At a past moment, Marta’s ongoing reading takes stava leggendo.
questions.speak: Alle nove Marta stava leggendo un libro.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I was cooking when you called.
questions.explanation: The cooking was underway before the completed call.
questions.speak: Io stavo cucinando quando hai chiamato.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: We were sleeping when the phone rang.
questions.answer: Stavamo dormendo quando è suonato il telefono.
questions.explanation: Stavamo dormendo is ongoing background; è suonato marks the interrupting event.
questions.speak: Stavamo dormendo quando è suonato il telefono.

questions.prompt: Use stare + gerundio to type the missing phrase.
questions.context: Ieri alle tre voi ___ al parco.
questions.translation: Yesterday at three you all were walking in the park.
questions.explanation: Voi takes stavate; camminare gives camminando.
questions.hint: Use the voi imperfect of stare.
questions.speak: Ieri alle tre voi stavate camminando al parco.

units.title: Reflexives and small pronouns
units.description: Keep the right person or thing in view without repeating each noun.

lessons.title: Describe your own routine
lessons.outcome: I can use a reflexive pronoun with a present-tense daily-routine verb.
lessons.takeaway: Mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si go before a finite reflexive verb and identify who receives the action.

objectives.label: Describe your own routine
objectives.explanation: Mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si go before a finite reflexive verb and identify who receives the action.

teach.title: Match pronoun and person
teach.body: Alzarsi gives mi alzo, ti alzi, si alza, ci alziamo, vi alzate, si alzano. The small pronoun is part of the verb phrase.

examples.en: I get up at seven.

teach.title: Everyday routines
teach.body: A reflexive verb often names a routine done to oneself: si sveglia, ci laviamo. Italian may use a reflexive where English does not.

examples.en: Anna wakes up early.

teach.tip: The reflexive pronoun sits before the finite verb in an ordinary statement.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I get up at seven.
questions.explanation: Io needs mi and the io verb form alzo.
questions.hint: Match both small pronoun and verb to io.
questions.speak: Io mi alzo alle sette.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: We wash up before dinner.
questions.explanation: Noi takes ci laviamo.
questions.speak: Noi ci laviamo prima di cena.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Marta wakes up early.
questions.explanation: Marta takes si before the finite verb.
questions.speak: Marta si sveglia presto.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Do you get up at eight?
questions.explanation: Tu takes ti alzi.
questions.hint: Use ti plus the tu form.
questions.speak: Tu ti alzi alle otto?

lessons.title: Tell a reflexive past event
lessons.outcome: I can use essere with a past reflexive verb and agree the participle.
lessons.takeaway: Reflexive passato prossimo uses a reflexive pronoun + essere + an agreeing participle.

objectives.label: Tell a reflexive past event
objectives.explanation: Reflexive passato prossimo uses a reflexive pronoun + essere + an agreeing participle.

teach.title: The three parts
teach.body: Mi sono alzato, ti sei alzata, si è alzato combine pronoun, essere, and participle.

examples.en: Yesterday I, a woman, woke up early.

teach.title: Agreement remains
teach.body: The participle matches the subject: le ragazze si sono alzate. With plural or feminine subjects, change the ending.

examples.it: I ragazzi si sono lavati le mani.
examples.en: The boys washed their hands.

teach.tip: The auxiliary is essere for reflexive verbs even when the non-reflexive verb uses avere.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Yesterday Anna got up early.
questions.explanation: Anna takes si è, and alzata agrees with her.
questions.speak: Ieri Anna si è alzata presto.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: We two women woke up at seven.
questions.explanation: Ci siamo is reflexive past; svegliate agrees with two women.
questions.speak: Noi due donne ci siamo svegliate alle sette.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I, a man, washed my hands.
questions.explanation: Reflexive past takes mi sono and masculine lavato here.
questions.speak: Mi sono lavato le mani.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: You, Marco, got up late yesterday.
questions.explanation: Marco is male: ti sei alzato.
questions.hint: Use the tu auxiliary sei and -o.
questions.speak: Tu, Marco, ti sei alzato tardi ieri.

lessons.title: Replace the thing seen
lessons.outcome: I can use lo, la, li, and le before a finite verb to avoid repeating a direct object.
lessons.takeaway: A direct-object pronoun replaces the person or thing acted on and agrees with that noun.

objectives.label: Replace the thing seen
objectives.explanation: A direct-object pronoun replaces the person or thing acted on and agrees with that noun.

teach.title: Singular things
teach.body: Lo replaces a masculine singular direct object; la replaces a feminine singular one. Place it before the finite verb.

examples.it: Vedi il libro? Sì, lo vedo.
examples.en: Do you see the book? Yes, I see it.

teach.title: Plural things
teach.body: Li replaces masculine plural objects; le replaces feminine plural objects. With non, say non lo vedo.

examples.it: Cerchi le chiavi? Le vedo qui.
examples.en: Are you looking for the keys? I see them here.

teach.tip: With a preceding direct object in a compound past tense, participle agreement needs extra care; that comes later.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am looking for the book. I cannot find it.
questions.explanation: Il libro is masculine singular, so lo replaces it.
questions.hint: Use the masculine singular object pronoun.
questions.speak: Cerco il libro. Non lo trovo.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Le, lo, and li replace the feminine plural, masculine singular, and masculine plural objects.
questions.hint: Match each pronoun to the noun it replaces.
questions.speak: Compro le mele e le porto a casa.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I see her from the window.
questions.explanation: La is the feminine direct object before vedo.
questions.speak: La vedo dalla finestra.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Do you have the tickets? Yes, I have them.
questions.explanation: I biglietti is masculine plural; li stands before ho.
questions.speak: Hai i biglietti? Sì, li ho.

lessons.title: Say to whom
lessons.outcome: I can use mi, ti, gli, and le for a receiver or addressee.
lessons.takeaway: An indirect-object pronoun often means to/for someone and normally goes before the finite verb.

objectives.label: Say to whom
objectives.explanation: An indirect-object pronoun often means to/for someone and normally goes before the finite verb.

teach.title: The recipient
teach.body: Mi means to me and ti to you. Gli means to him; le means to her in the common singular pattern.

examples.en: Marco gives me the book.

teach.title: With speaking verbs
teach.body: Dire and telefonare often take a recipient: gli dico la verità, le telefono. Keep the message or thing separate from the person receiving it.

examples.en: I will call her tomorrow.

teach.tip: In the common singular pattern, le refers to her; context identifies the person.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I speak to Luca. I will speak to him tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Luca is the male addressee, so gli means to him.
questions.hint: This is to him, not a direct object.
questions.speak: Parlo a Luca. Gli parlo domani.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Do il libro a Marta. ___ do il libro.
questions.translation: I give the book to Marta. I give her the book.
questions.explanation: Marta is the female recipient, so le means to her.
questions.hint: Choose the indirect form for her.
questions.speak: Do il libro a Marta. Le do il libro.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I send you a photo.
questions.explanation: Ti means to you and goes before mando.
questions.speak: Ti mando una foto.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Anna parla a me. Anna ___ parla.
questions.translation: Anna speaks to me. Anna speaks to me.
questions.explanation: Mi means to me before parla.
questions.speak: Anna parla a me. Anna mi parla.

lessons.title: Place a pronoun with an infinitive
lessons.outcome: I can place a direct-object pronoun before a modal or attach it to the infinitive.
lessons.takeaway: With a modal + infinitive, either lo voglio leggere or voglio leggerlo can express the same object.

objectives.label: Place a pronoun with an infinitive
objectives.explanation: With a modal + infinitive, either lo voglio leggere or voglio leggerlo can express the same object.

teach.title: Before the modal
teach.body: Lo voglio leggere places lo before the finite modal. Non goes before the pronoun: non lo posso comprare.

examples.en: I want to read it tonight.

teach.title: After the infinitive
teach.body: Voglio leggerlo attaches the pronoun to the infinitive after removing its final -e. These two placements are common alternatives.

examples.en: I want to read it tonight.

teach.tip: Do not attach lo to the conjugated modal.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: This book is interesting: I want to read it tonight.
questions.explanation: Attach lo to the infinitive after dropping final -e.
questions.speak: Questo libro è interessante: voglio leggerlo stasera.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Il biglietto è caro: non ___ comprare.
questions.translation: The ticket is expensive: I cannot buy it.
questions.explanation: Lo replaces masculine biglietto and stands before posso.
questions.hint: Place the pronoun before the finite modal.
questions.speak: Il biglietto è caro: non lo posso comprare.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I have to call her today.
questions.explanation: La can stand before devo in a modal + infinitive phrase.
questions.speak: La devo chiamare oggi.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: The film is good; I want to see it tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Vedere drops its final -e when lo attaches: vederlo.
questions.speak: Il film è bello; voglio vederlo domani.

units.title: Future and polite possibilities
units.description: Make a future plan and soften a request with a conditional form.

lessons.title: Make a future plan
lessons.outcome: I can form the regular future of common -are, -ere, and -ire verbs.
lessons.takeaway: Future endings are -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno; -are uses e in its future stem.

objectives.label: Make a future plan
objectives.explanation: Future endings are -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno; -are uses e in its future stem.

teach.title: The shared endings
teach.body: Parlare gives parlerò, parlerai, parlerà; the -are vowel becomes e. The plural includes parleremo, parlerete, parleranno.

examples.en: Tomorrow I will speak with Marco.

teach.title: Other regular families
teach.body: Prendere gives prenderò, partire gives partirò. Italian also often uses the present for near plans, but the future makes futurity explicit.

examples.en: Next week we will leave.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Tomorrow we will speak Italian.
questions.explanation: Parlare takes the future stem parler- and noi ending -emo.
questions.hint: Use parler- plus the we ending.
questions.speak: Domani noi parleremo italiano.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Tomorrow Marta will take the train.
questions.explanation: Prendere takes the future stem prender- and third-person -à.
questions.speak: Domani Marta prenderà il treno.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: They will leave on Monday morning.
questions.explanation: Partiranno has the third-person plural future ending.
questions.speak: Partiranno lunedì mattina.

questions.prompt: Use the future tense to type the missing form.
questions.translation: I will finish the work tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Finire takes the future ending -ò.
questions.hint: Use finir- plus the I ending.
questions.speak: Io finirò il lavoro domani.

lessons.title: Use common irregular futures
lessons.outcome: I can use future stems of essere, avere, andare, fare, and venire.
lessons.takeaway: Some common futures keep regular endings but change their stems: sar-, avr-, andr-, far-, verr-.

objectives.label: Use common irregular futures
objectives.explanation: Some common futures keep regular endings but change their stems: sar-, avr-, andr-, far-, verr-.

teach.title: Short future stems
teach.body: Essere → sarò, avere → avrò, andare → andrò. The future ending still tells the person.

examples.en: Tomorrow I will be at home.

teach.title: More useful stems
teach.body: Fare → farò and venire → verrò. For a plural subject: faremo, verranno.

examples.en: They will come on Saturday.

teach.tip: Keep the doubled r in verrò and verranno.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Tomorrow I will go to Milan.
questions.explanation: Andare uses the future stem andr-.
questions.speak: Domani io andrò a Milano.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Avere keeps the future stem avr- while its ending changes with the person.
questions.speak: Io avrò tempo domani.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Luca will be here soon.
questions.explanation: Sarà is the future third-person form of essere.
questions.hint: Put the future verb after Luca.
questions.speak: Luca sarà qui presto.

questions.prompt: Use the future tense to type the missing form.
questions.translation: Marta and Luca will make dinner.
questions.explanation: Fare has future stem far- and third-person plural -anno.
questions.speak: Marta e Luca faranno la cena.

lessons.title: Ask more politely
lessons.outcome: I can use vorrei, potrei, and potrebbe in courteous requests and simple possibilities.
lessons.takeaway: The present conditional softens a wish or request: vorrei, potrei, and polite Lei potrebbe.

objectives.label: Ask more politely
objectives.explanation: The present conditional softens a wish or request: vorrei, potrei, and polite Lei potrebbe.

teach.title: A softer wish
teach.body: Vorrei + a noun or infinitive is a polite “I would like.” Contrast the direct voglio.

examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

teach.title: A possible action
teach.body: Potrei + infinitive means “I could.” Potrebbe + infinitive politely asks one person addressed as Lei. Mi piacerebbe + infinitive expresses a wish.

examples.en: Could I pay by card?

teach.tip: These are present conditional forms, even though English uses “would/could.”

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Al bar: ___ un tè, per favore.
questions.translation: At the café: I would like a tea, please.
questions.explanation: Vorrei is the polite conditional request.
questions.hint: Choose the form meaning “I would like.”
questions.speak: Al bar: vorrei un tè, per favore.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Could I open the window?
questions.explanation: Potrei expresses a softened possibility or request.
questions.speak: Potrei aprire la finestra?

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I would like to visit Rome.
questions.explanation: Mi piacerebbe introduces a desired action.
questions.speak: Mi piacerebbe visitare Roma.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Madam, could you give me a glass of water?
questions.explanation: Potrebbe is the courteous Lei form; darmi means “give me.”
questions.hint: Use polite Lei plus an infinitive with mi attached.
questions.speak: Signora, potrebbe darmi un bicchiere d’acqua?

units.title: Compare and measure
units.description: Compare people and things, then describe a useful amount.

lessons.title: Compare two things
lessons.outcome: I can use più/meno ... di for two people or things and ... che for two qualities or actions.
lessons.takeaway: Use di before the second compared noun; che joins two qualities or two actions for the same referent.

objectives.label: Compare two things
objectives.explanation: Use di before the second compared noun; che joins two qualities or two actions for the same referent.

teach.title: Two people or things
teach.body: Use più or meno + adjective + di to compare two different people or things. Contract di + article when needed.

examples.it: Luca è più alto di Marco.
examples.en: Luca is taller than Marco.

teach.title: Two features or actions
teach.body: When comparing two qualities of the same thing, use che: più comodo che elegante. The comparison is within one referent.

examples.it: Questo divano è più comodo che bello.
examples.en: This sofa is more comfortable than beautiful.

teach.tip: Some comparisons have irregular words such as migliore; learn those later.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Sara is taller than Anna.
questions.explanation: Two different people are compared: Sara and Anna.
questions.hint: Use di before the second person.
questions.speak: Sara è più alta di Anna.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Questo zaino è più pratico ___ elegante.
questions.translation: This backpack is more practical than elegant.
questions.explanation: Pratico and elegante are two qualities of the same backpack.
questions.speak: Questo zaino è più pratico che elegante.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: The train is less slow than the bus.
questions.answer: Il treno è più veloce dell’autobus.
questions.explanation: Di + l’autobus contracts to dell’autobus after a comparison.
questions.speak: Il treno è più veloce dell’autobus.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Questa stanza è più grande ___ cucina.
questions.translation: This room is bigger than the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Di + la cucina contracts to della.
questions.hint: Use di plus the feminine article.
questions.speak: Questa stanza è più grande della cucina.

lessons.title: Pick the highest degree
lessons.outcome: I can say “the most” in a group and intensify an adjective with -issimo.
lessons.takeaway: Il/la più ... di marks a relative superlative; -issimo intensifies a quality without comparing a group.

objectives.label: Pick the highest degree
objectives.explanation: Il/la più ... di marks a relative superlative; -issimo intensifies a quality without comparing a group.

teach.title: Highest in a group
teach.body: Use article + più + adjective + di/in to pick one within a group: la più alta della classe.

examples.it: Marta è la più alta della classe.
examples.en: Marta is the tallest in the class.

teach.title: Very, without a group
teach.body: Add -issimo/-issima/-issimi/-issime to many adjectives for a strong degree: bellissima. It agrees with the noun.

examples.en: These shoes are extremely comfortable.

teach.tip: Molto bello also means very beautiful, but does not select one from a group.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Marta is the fastest on the team.
questions.explanation: Marta is feminine singular and this selects one person from a group.
questions.speak: Marta è la più veloce della squadra.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: These cakes are extremely good.
questions.explanation: Torte is feminine plural, so buonissime agrees.
questions.speak: Queste torte sono buonissime.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Luca is the youngest in the family.
questions.answer: Luca è il più giovane della famiglia.
questions.explanation: Il più giovane selects Luca from the family group.
questions.hint: Keep il più together before the adjective.
questions.speak: Luca è il più giovane della famiglia.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: The house is extremely beautiful.
questions.explanation: Bella takes -issima for feminine singular intensity; molto bella is also natural.
questions.hint: Use the feminine singular intensive form.
questions.speak: La casa è bellissima.

lessons.title: Use approximate amounts
lessons.outcome: I can choose qualche, alcuni/alcune, troppo, and un po’ di with suitable nouns.
lessons.takeaway: Qualche takes a singular count noun; alcuni/alcune take plural nouns; troppo agrees when it modifies a noun.

objectives.label: Use approximate amounts
objectives.explanation: Qualche takes a singular count noun; alcuni/alcune take plural nouns; troppo agrees when it modifies a noun.

teach.title: Some: singular or plural
teach.body: Qualche always precedes a singular count noun: qualche libro. Alcuni libri and alcune case use plural nouns.

examples.en: I bought a few books.

teach.title: Too much and a little
teach.body: Troppo agrees with a noun: troppi libri, troppa acqua. Un po’ di works for a modest amount of a mass noun.

examples.en: There is too much sugar in the coffee.

teach.tip: Qualche is not followed by a plural noun.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I would like a few apples for the trip.
questions.explanation: Qualche is followed by singular mela despite plural meaning.
questions.hint: Look at the noun form mela.
questions.speak: Vorrei qualche mela per il viaggio.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Troppo agrees with persone, libri, and acqua in gender and number.
questions.speak: Ci sono troppe persone in questa stanza.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I have some ideas for dinner.
questions.answer: Ho alcune idee per la cena.
questions.explanation: Alcune accompanies plural feminine idee.
questions.speak: Ho alcune idee per la cena.

questions.prompt: Use un po’ di to type the missing phrase.
questions.translation: I put a little milk in the coffee.
questions.explanation: Un po’ di introduces a small amount of the mass noun latte.
questions.hint: Use the fixed phrase before latte.
questions.speak: Metto un po’ di latte nel caffè.

units.title: Commands, prepositions, and links
units.description: Give clear directions and connect two small ideas in a useful sentence.

lessons.title: Address one person politely
lessons.outcome: I can give a courteous Lei instruction with a common command form.
lessons.takeaway: A formal Lei command uses a present subjunctive-shaped form such as parli, prenda, venga.

objectives.label: Address one person politely
objectives.explanation: A formal Lei command uses a present subjunctive-shaped form such as parli, prenda, venga.

teach.title: Lei commands
teach.body: For a person addressed as Lei, say Parli più piano, Prenda posto, Venga qui. The form differs from familiar tu commands.

examples.en: Please take a seat, madam.

teach.title: Keep the register consistent
teach.body: Use a formal form with signora, dottore, or a stranger. For -are, Lei often ends in -i; for -ere/-ire, commonly -a.

examples.it: Mi dica il suo nome, per favore.
examples.en: Please tell me your name.

teach.tip: Dica is the irregular formal command of dire.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Madam, come here, please.
questions.explanation: Venga is the polite Lei command of venire.
questions.speak: Signora, venga qui, per favore.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Doctor, speak more slowly, please.
questions.explanation: Parli is the formal Lei command of parlare.
questions.speak: Dottore, parli più piano, per favore.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Please take a seat, madam.
questions.explanation: Prenda is a formal singular command.
questions.speak: Prenda posto, signora.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Signora, mi ___ il suo nome, per favore.
questions.translation: Madam, please tell me your name.
questions.explanation: Dica is the courteous Lei command of dire.
questions.hint: Use the polite command of dire.
questions.speak: Signora, mi dica il suo nome, per favore.

lessons.title: Tell someone not to do it
lessons.outcome: I can form a negative tu command and place an object pronoun naturally.
lessons.takeaway: For tu, use non + infinitive; with a pronoun, both non lo prendere and non prenderlo are possible.

objectives.label: Tell someone not to do it
objectives.explanation: For tu, use non + infinitive; with a pronoun, both non lo prendere and non prenderlo are possible.

teach.title: Negative tu
teach.body: Unlike the positive tu command, the negative uses non + infinitive: non parlare, non entrare.

examples.en: Do not come in now.

teach.title: With a small pronoun
teach.body: A pronoun can precede the infinitive or attach to it: non lo prendere / non prenderlo. Keep non first.

examples.en: Do not take it; it is broken.

teach.tip: For voi, use non + the voi command: Non entrate.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Marco, do not speak so loudly.
questions.explanation: The informal singular negative command is non + infinitive.
questions.hint: Use the whole infinitive after non.
questions.speak: Marco, non parlare così forte.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.translation: Everyday Italian sentences.
questions.explanation: Tu uses non + infinitive; voi and polite Lei use their corresponding command forms.
questions.hint: Match each addressee to the command form.
questions.speak: Marco, non parlare così forte.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Do not take it; it is broken.
questions.explanation: Lo can go before the negative tu infinitive.
questions.speak: Non lo prendere, è rotto.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Lucia, do not open the door.
questions.explanation: Negative tu uses non + infinitive aprire.
questions.hint: Use the infinitive, not the affirmative command.
questions.speak: Lucia, non aprire la porta.

lessons.title: Use da for source, person, and duration
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish da for origin, visiting a person, and a duration continuing now.
lessons.takeaway: Da can mean from, at someone’s place, or since/for when an action continues to now.

objectives.label: Use da for source, person, and duration
objectives.explanation: Da can mean from, at someone’s place, or since/for when an action continues to now.

teach.title: From and to a person
teach.body: Vengo da Milano marks origin; vado da Marco means going to Marco’s place or presence. With an article, da + il is dal.

examples.en: Tonight I am going to Luca’s place.

teach.title: Since or for, still continuing
teach.body: Studio italiano da due anni means I have studied Italian for two years and still do. Use present tense for the ongoing situation.

examples.en: I have lived here for three years.

teach.tip: Do not copy an English present perfect automatically in this pattern.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Tomorrow I am going to the dentist.
questions.explanation: Da + il dentista becomes dal dentista, a visit to the person.
questions.speak: Domani vado dal dentista.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I have lived in Turin for five years and still live there.
questions.explanation: For a duration continuing now, Italian uses present + da.
questions.speak: Abito a Torino da cinque anni.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I come from Naples.
questions.explanation: Da marks the city of origin.
questions.speak: Vengo da Napoli.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Sara is at the doctor’s office now.
questions.explanation: Da + il medico contracts to dal.
questions.hint: She is at the person’s place.
questions.speak: Sara è dal medico adesso.

lessons.title: Connect cause and sequence
lessons.outcome: I can link short ideas with perché, quindi, poi, and mentre.
lessons.takeaway: Perché gives a cause; quindi a result; poi a next step; mentre joins simultaneous actions.

objectives.label: Connect cause and sequence
objectives.explanation: Perché gives a cause; quindi a result; poi a next step; mentre joins simultaneous actions.

teach.title: Cause and result
teach.body: Use perché for why something happens and quindi for its consequence. They organize the same facts from different directions.

examples.en: It is raining, so I am staying home.

teach.title: Next and simultaneous
teach.body: Poi orders the next event. Mentre introduces something happening at the same time and often leads to an imperfect past background.

examples.it: Preparo il tè mentre Luca legge.
examples.en: I make tea while Luca reads.

teach.tip: Use commas to help a reader follow two clauses.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am hungry, so I prepare dinner.
questions.explanation: The second clause is the result of being hungry.
questions.speak: Ho fame, quindi preparo la cena.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am staying home because it is raining.
questions.explanation: The rain is the reason for staying home.
questions.speak: Resto a casa perché piove.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: First I buy bread, then I return home.
questions.answer: Prima compro il pane, poi torno a casa.
questions.explanation: Poi marks the next step after buying bread.
questions.speak: Prima compro il pane, poi torno a casa.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Luca reads while I cook.
questions.explanation: Mentre links simultaneous actions.
questions.speak: Luca legge mentre io cucino.

lessons.title: Add one detail with che
lessons.outcome: I can join a noun to a simple describing clause with che.
lessons.takeaway: Che is the same relative word for male, female, singular, and plural antecedents.

objectives.label: Add one detail with che
objectives.explanation: Che is the same relative word for male, female, singular, and plural antecedents.

teach.title: Describe the person
teach.body: Che connects a noun to information about it: la ragazza che parla. The finite verb in the added clause has its own subject.

examples.it: La ragazza che parla è mia sorella.
examples.en: The girl who is speaking is my sister.

teach.title: Describe a thing
teach.body: Che can also mean that/which for a thing: il libro che leggo. It does not change form with libro or libri.

examples.it: Il libro che leggo è interessante.
examples.en: The book I am reading is interesting.

teach.tip: Do not confuse this relative che with the comparative che.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: La donna ___ parla è mia madre.
questions.translation: The woman who is speaking is my mother.
questions.explanation: Che links donna to the clause that identifies her.
questions.speak: La donna che parla è mia madre.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: The books that I am looking for are here.
questions.explanation: Che stays the same with plural libri.
questions.hint: The relative form does not change for plural.
questions.speak: I libri che cerco sono qui.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: The train that leaves at eight is full.
questions.answer: Il treno che parte alle otto è pieno.
questions.explanation: Che introduces the identifying clause about il treno.
questions.hint: Put che directly after the noun.
questions.speak: Il treno che parte alle otto è pieno.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: I know the girl who works here.
questions.explanation: Che joins ragazza with the clause lavora qui.
questions.hint: Use the same relative form for feminine nouns.
questions.speak: Conosco la ragazza che lavora qui.
